neighbours.label: the first word of an explanation of what an expression or utterance means ('it means that he...', 'it implies that...'); 'which means that' consequences stay low
fire: If a friend says she is under the weather, it means that she feels a little sick.
When your boss says the door is always open, it means that you can talk to him any time.
The phrase 'break a leg' sounds odd, but it means that you wish someone good luck.
Calling someone 'cold' is not about temperature; it implies that they show little feeling.
If the sign says 'no vacancy', it means that the hotel has no free rooms.
The word 'frugal' is kinder than 'cheap', for it suggests that a person spends wisely.
When a dog wags its tail slowly, it often means that it is unsure, not happy.
In English, 'I'm all ears' is polite; it means that you are listening closely.
quiet: My friend was sick last week, so she stayed home and slept most of the day.
The office door is always open, and people walk in and out all day long.
The new road is finished, which means that the drive to town is much shorter.
The weather turned cold last night, and the lake froze near the shore.
The hotel was full, so we drove another hour to find a free room.
Prices went up again this month, which means that families will spend more on food.
The dog wagged its tail and ran to the door when it heard the car.
She was all ears during the lecture and took careful notes in her notebook.
